claim: Aquatic birds are the main reservoir of influenza A viruses in nature.
source: Aquatic birds are the main reservoir of influenza A viruses in nature (Krauss and Webster, 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Krauss and Webster, 2010

claim: Influenza viruses from aquatic birds sporadically enter terrestrial bird and mammalian host populations and achieve sustained circulation in these new hosts.
source: Influenza viruses from aquatic birds sporadically enter terrestrial bird and mammalian host populations and achieve sustained circulation in these new hosts (Vandegrift et al., 2010), sometimes after reassortment with influenza viruses already circulating in the new host (Webster et al., 1992).
evidence: Supported by citations to Vandegrift et al., 2010 and Webster et al., 1992

claim: Adaptation of viruses from aquatic birds to mammals involves a change in tissue tropism from intestinal to respiratory epithelia.
source: Adaptation of viruses from aquatic birds to mammals involves a change in tissue tropism from intestinal to respiratory epithelia (Hinshaw et al., 1979; Hénaux and Samuel, 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Hinshaw et al., 1979 and Hénaux and Samuel, 2015

claim: More than one thousand human infections with avian influenza viruses were detected in the last decade, for example H5N1 and H7N9.
source: More than one thousand human infections with avian influenza viruses were detected in the last decade, for example H5N1 and H7N9 (Qin et al., 2015)
evidence: Supported by citation to Qin et al., 2015

claim: An H3N2 variant spilled over into humans attending agricultural shows in the early 2010s.
source: as well as swine influenza viruses, e.g. an H3N2 variant that spilled over into humans attending agricultural shows in the early 2010s, H3N2v (Jhung et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Jhung et al., 2013

claim: Zoonotic infections with H7N7 from poultry or wild birds have occurred.
source: In addition, zoonotic infections with other viruses from poultry or wild birds have occurred, including for example H7N7 (Fouchier et al., 2004)
evidence: Supported by citation to Fouchier et al., 2004

claim: Zoonotic infections with H10N8 from poultry or wild birds have occurred.
source: H10N8 (Wohlbold et al., 2015)
evidence: Supported by citation to Wohlbold et al., 2015

claim: Zoonotic infections with H6N1 from poultry or wild birds have occurred.
source: H6N1 (Wei et al., 2013)
evidence: Supported by citation to Wei et al., 2013

claim: Zoonotic infections with H9N2 from poultry or wild birds have occurred.
source: H9N2 (Butt et al., 2005)
evidence: Supported by citation to Butt et al., 2005

claim: Zoonotic infections with H5N6 from poultry or wild birds have occurred.
source: and H5N6 (Yang et al., 2015)
evidence: Supported by citation to Yang et al., 2015

claim: The severity of zoonotic influenza A infections ranges from clinically inapparent to fatal.
source: The severity of zoonotic influenza A infections ranges from clinically inapparent (Gomaa et al., 2015; To et al., 2016) to fatal (de Jong et al., 2006; Gao et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Gomaa et al., 2015; To et al., 2016; de Jong et al., 2006; Gao et al., 2013

claim: Secondary transmission can occur following some spillover events.
source: Although secondary transmission can occur following some of these spillover events (Kucharski et al., 2014)
evidence: Supported by citation to Kucharski et al., 2014

claim: Only four spillover events in the last hundred years led to sustained person-to-person transmission with global spread.
source: only a very small proportion of them—four in the last hundred years, which seems to be close to the historical average (Patterson, 1986)—led to sustained person-to-person transmission with global spread (Box 1).
evidence: Supported by citation to Patterson, 1986

claim: There are 18 known HA types and 11 known NA types.
source: There are 18 known HA types and 11 known NA types (Tong et al., 2013)
evidence: Supported by citation to Tong et al., 2013

claim: Sustained spread in humans has been limited to the H1N1, H2N2, and H3N2 subtypes.
source: So far, sustained spread in humans has been limited to the H1N1, H2N2, and H3N2 subtypes (Kuiken et al., 2006)
evidence: Supported by citation to Kuiken et al., 2006

claim: It is possible that other subtypes circulated prior to 1918.
source: though it is possible that other subtypes circulated prior to 1918, the year of the first pandemic from which viruses are available for study (Worobey et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Worobey et al., 2014

claim: Multiple virus–host interactions are necessary for replication and onward transmission.
source: Multiple virus–host interactions are necessary for replication and onward transmission; the differences in the genetic requirements to accomplish each of these interactions in humans versus other animals provide a barrier to sustained transmission following spillover (Russell et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Russell et al., 2014

claim: Droplet transmission in ferrets is a useful, albeit imperfect, correlate of the potential of influenza strains to transmit efficiently in human populations.
source: Droplet transmission in ferrets is a useful, albeit imperfect, correlate of the potential of influenza strains to transmit efficiently in human populations (Buhnerkempe et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Buhnerkempe et al., 2015

claim: Certain specific traits associated with mammalian host adaptation were required to achieve respiratory droplet transmission in ferrets.
source: Starting from an zoonotic highly pathogenic avian influenza isolate from a human case of infection (or a reassortant of the HA from a different zoonotic H5N1 highly pathogenic avian influenza isolate, with the other segments from the 2009 pandemic H1N1 strain), it was shown that certain specific traits that had been previously associated with mammalian host adaptation were required to achieve respiratory droplet transmission.
evidence: Inferred from experimental studies described in the text

claim: Ferret-transmission phenotypes were associated with certain genetic changes relative to the original avian viruses in HA and polymerase-complex proteins.
source: These ferret-transmission phenotypes in turn were associated with certain genetic changes relative to the original avian viruses (Imai et al., 2012; Herfst et al., 2012; Linster et al., 2014). These specific changes occur both in HA and in polymerase-complex proteins.
evidence: Supported by citations to Imai et al., 2012; Herfst et al., 2012; Linster et al., 2014

claim: Changes identified in adaptation to ferret transmission would also be important for adaptation to sustained transmission in humans.
source: The rationale for these experiments was that, because the ferret model recapitulates many features of human infection, changes identified in adaptation to ferret transmission would also be important for adaptation to sustained transmission in humans (Davis et al., 2014; Schultz-Cherry et al., 2014), though this can never be known with certainty (Palese and Wang, 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Davis et al., 2014; Schultz-Cherry et al., 2014; and Palese and Wang, 2012

claim: Viruses isolated from humans who were infected by contact with birds show some changes associated with mammalian adaptation.
source: Notably, viruses isolated from humans who were infected by contact with birds show some of these changes (Russell et al., 2012; Bi et al., 2015), particularly the change at amino acid 627 of the PB2 gene (Jonges et al., 2014; Chen et al., 2014; Fonville et al., 2013)
evidence: Supported by citations to Russell et al., 2012; Bi et al., 2015; Jonges et al., 2014; Chen et al., 2014; Fonville et al., 2013

claim: The change at amino acid 627 of the PB2 gene often affects polymerase complex efficiency.
source: particularly the change at amino acid 627 of the PB2 gene (Jonges et al., 2014; Chen et al., 2014; Fonville et al., 2013), which often affects polymerase complex efficiency (see below).
evidence: Supported by citations and reference to later section

claim: Even the first generation of human infection from nonhuman hosts can initiate a process of host adaptation.
source: This indicates that even the first generation of human infection from nonhuman hosts can initiate a process of host adaptation.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that viruses from first human infections show adaptive changes

claim: Not all the human-adaptive changes must be in place in the avian reservoir to initiate the process of host adaptation.
source: It also indicates that not all the human-adaptive changes must be in place in the avian reservoir to initiate this process.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that adaptation can occur after initial human infection

claim: Some human infections involve viruses that are not yet fully human-adapted.
source: Some human infections, including some zoonotic cases (de Jong et al., 2006; Chen et al., 2014, 2006; Sha et al., 2016) and some cases early in a pandemic (Rogers and D'Souza, 1989; Connor et al., 1994; Stevens et al., 2006; Glaser et al., 2005; Pappas et al., 2010), involve viruses that are not yet fully human-adapted (see below and Tables 2–4).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to Rogers and D'Souza, 1989; Connor et al., 1994; Stevens et al., 2006; Glaser et al., 2005; Pappas et al., 2010; de Jong et al., 2006; Chen et al., 2014, 2006; Sha et al., 2016

claim: The interpretation of some isolates is complicated by uncertainty about whether they were passaged in hen's eggs at some point in their history.
source: The interpretation of some of these isolates is complicated by uncertainty about whether they were passaged in hen's eggs at some point in their history.
evidence: Acknowledged limitation in interpreting historical data

claim: Certain types of countermeasures against an influenza pandemic are effective only against one lineage of viruses.
source: Certain types of countermeasures against an influenza pandemic are effective only against one lineage of viruses – for example, creating stockpiles or seed stocks of vaccines against a particular subtype, or culling poultry infected with that subtype.
evidence: Based on established knowledge about vaccine specificity and control measures

claim: It is not currently feasible to invest in countermeasures against all viruses circulating in avian or other reservoirs.
source: It is not currently feasible to invest in such countermeasures against all viruses circulating in avian or other reservoirs, or even against all those causing known zoonotic cases.
evidence: Based on practical and resource constraints

claim: There would be value in an accurate system to assess the relative pandemic risks posed by each virus.
source: Therefore, there would be value in an accurate system to assess the relative pandemic risks posed by each virus and prioritize them for the development of such strain-specific countermeasures, while directing fewer resources to strains of lower concern (Kaplan et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kaplan et al., 2016 and logical reasoning

claim: The CDC's Influenza Risk Assessment Tool (IRAT) incorporates elements including properties of the virus, field and epidemiological findings, and attributes of the human population.
source: One response is the CDC's Influenza Risk Assessment Tool (IRAT) (Trock et al., 2015), which incorporates elements including properties of the virus, field and epidemiological findings, and attributes of the human population to provide a framework to differentiate among novel influenza viruses thought to possess pandemic potential.
evidence: Supported by citation to Trock et al., 2015

claim: Risk assessments can help focus pandemic prevention and response efforts on the viruses thought to pose the highest risk of pandemic spread.
source: Such risk assessments can help focus pandemic prevention and response efforts on the viruses thought to pose the highest risk of pandemic spread (Davis et al., 2014)
evidence: Supported by citation to Davis et al., 2014

claim: Influenza pandemics are rare events.
source: These difficulties are exacerbated by the fact that influenza pandemics are rare events, and that risk assessments are not yet made with enough quantitative precision to formally evaluate their practical application.
evidence: Based on historical observation of pandemic frequency

claim: Perfect information about the viral determinants of pandemic risk might only be enough to distinguish between strains with a low risk and those with an extremely low risk.
source: Even perfect information about the viral determinants of pandemic risk might only be enough to distinguish between strains with a low risk of causing a pandemic (say, 0.1% per year) and those with an extremely low risk (say, less than 0.01% per year), with unpredictable ecological or evolutionary contingencies determining which of these low-probability events will actually occur.
evidence: Speculative reasoning about the limits of prediction

claim: An avian influenza virus could acquire one or more of the determinants of pandemic potential by reassorting with a human seasonal influenza virus.
source: One such contingency is that an avian influenza virus could acquire one or more of the determinants of pandemic potential by reassorting with a human seasonal influenza virus.
evidence: Based on known mechanisms of influenza evolution

claim: With only one pandemic every few decades, the data set for testing the prediction of such rare events is inadequate.
source: With only one pandemic every few decades, the data set for testing the prediction of such rare events is inadequate, a problem that challenges predictions in many fields beyond infectious diseases (King and Zeng, 2001; Hansson, 2006).
evidence: Supported by citations to King and Zeng, 2001; Hansson, 2006

claim: Evolutionary events in which a strain increases human-to-human transmissibility, but not enough to spark a pandemic, are extremely hard to observe.
source: Evolutionary events in which a strain increases human-to-human transmissibility, but not enough to spark a pandemic, are extremely hard to observe, but if we could do so it would increase our ability to characterize the process of adaptation (Kucharski et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kucharski et al., 2015 and logical reasoning

claim: HA receptor binding specificity, HA pH of activation, and polymerase complex activity span the viral life cycle.
source: we considered in detail the present state of knowledge concerning three phenotypic traits: HA receptor binding specificity, and HA pH of activation, and polymerase complex activity, (Figure 1). These were chosen from a longer list of candidate traits (Table 1) because they span the viral life cycle (Figure 1) and their role in host adaptation has been extensively studied.
evidence: Stated in text and illustrated in Figure 1

claim: All three traits (HA receptor binding specificity, HA pH of activation, and polymerase complex activity) are believed to be required for an influenza virus to cause a pandemic.
source: All three are believed to be required for an influenza virus to cause a pandemic; consistent with this assumption, all three traits have been present to some degree in the earliest viruses isolated in pandemics since the 20th century, though some have been enhanced by subsequent evolution during seasonal transmission in humans.
evidence: Based on analysis of pandemic viruses and established understanding

claim: For each of the three traits (HA receptor binding specificity, HA pH of activation, and polymerase complex activity), viruses isolated from avian hosts typically do not show the mammalian-adapted phenotype.
source: Moreover, for each of these three traits, viruses isolated from avian hosts typically do not show the mammalian-adapted phenotype, reflecting divergent selection pressures in the two classes of hosts (Tables 2, 3, and 4).
evidence: Stated in text and supported by data in Tables 2, 3, and 4

claim: All three traits (HA receptor binding specificity, HA pH of activation, and polymerase complex activity) changed in the adaptation of zoonotic H5 influenza viruses to droplet transmission in ferrets.
source: All three traits changed in the adaptation of zoonotic H5 influenza viruses to droplet transmission in ferrets (Imai et al., 2012; Linster et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Imai et al., 2012; Linster et al., 2014

claim: Each of the three traits (HA receptor binding specificity, HA pH of activation, and polymerase complex activity) is quantitative.
source: We emphasize that each of these traits is quantitative, and that human-adaptation is not a threshold criterion but a continuum
evidence: Stated as a conceptual clarification

claim: Attachment of an influenza virus to a host cell requires binding of the viral HA to a sialylated glycan receptor (sialic acid) on the surface of the host cell.
source: Attachment of an influenza virus to a host cell requires binding of the viral HA to a sialylated glycan receptor (sialic acid) on the surface of the host cell.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of influenza virus biology

claim: Cells of the avian gut and a minority of cells in deep lung in mammals predominantly express receptors terminated with an α2,3-linked sialic acid.
source: Cells of the avian gut and a minority of cells in deep lung in mammals predominantly express receptors terminated with an α2,3-linked sialic acid: hereafter, α2,3 glycans or avian receptors (Russell et al., 2006; Gambaryan et al., 1997; van Riel et al., 2006; Shinya et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citations to Russell et al., 2006; Gambaryan et al., 1997; van Riel et al., 2006; Shinya et al., 2006

claim: In humans and other mammals, upper respiratory epithelial cells express mainly glycan receptors terminated by α2,6-linked sialic acid.
source: By contrast, in humans and other mammals, upper respiratory epithelial cells express mainly glycan receptors terminated by α2,6-linked sialic acid: α2,6 glycans or human receptors (Stevens et al., 2006; Shinya et al., 2006; Chandrasekaran et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to Stevens et al., 2006; Shinya et al., 2006; Chandrasekaran et al., 2008

claim: The human upper respiratory epithelium is the primary target site for infection of human-adapted viruses.
source: The human upper respiratory epithelium is the primary target site for infection of human-adapted viruses, and infection at this site is thought to be a prerequisite for efficient human-to-human transmission via respiratory droplets.
evidence: Based on established understanding of influenza transmission

claim: Human adaptation of an HA is associated with a switch in its binding preference from avian to human receptors.
source: Thus, it appears that human adaptation of an HA is associated with a switch in its binding preference from avian to human receptors.
evidence: Inferred from the distribution of receptors and infection patterns

claim: Receptor binding preference is defined as the ratio of affinity (or avidity) of an HA molecule for an α2,6 glycan relative to that for an α2,3 glycan.
source: Receptor binding preference is defined as the ratio of affinity (or avidity) of an HA molecule for an α2,6 glycan relative to that for an α2,3 glycan, with higher values associated with greater human adaptation.
evidence: Definition provided in the text

claim: The evolution of receptor binding specificity is driven by the host environment, with selection for specificity during the infection process within a host and during the process of transmission.
source: The evolution of receptor binding specificity is driven by the host environment, with selection for specificity during the infection process within a host and during the process of transmission.
evidence: Based on understanding of evolutionary processes

claim: The error-prone replication of influenza genomes can facilitate rapid emergence of viruses with amino acid substitutions that alter the receptor binding characteristics of the HA.
source: The error-prone replication of influenza genomes can facilitate rapid emergence of viruses with amino acid substitutions that alter the receptor binding characteristics of the HA (Lakdawala et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lakdawala et al., 2015

claim: Recent experimental evidence in ferrets implicates the soft palate as an important site of selection for α2,6 specificity.
source: Recent experimental evidence in ferrets implicates the soft palate as an important site of selection for α2,6 specificity (Lakdawala et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lakdawala et al., 2015

claim: Preference for binding human or avian glycan receptors is determined by the structure of the viral HA.
source: Preference for binding human or avian glycan receptors is determined by the structure of the viral HA.
evidence: Based on structural biology knowledge

claim: Antigenic regions of the HA are located nearby regions that determine receptor-binding preference.
source: Importantly, antigenic regions of the HA are located nearby regions that determine receptor-binding preference, meaning that selection for antigenic escape may be constrained by the need to maintain receptor preference (Koel et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Koel et al., 2013

claim: There is evidence that avian- or human-adapted HA bind to different conformations of the avian and human receptors: the cis conformation of human receptors and the trans conformation of avian receptors.
source: Although the co-crystal structures of HA and sialylated glycans have not been solved for all pairs, there is evidence that avian- or human-adapted HA bind to different conformations of the avian and human receptors: the cis conformation of human receptors and the trans conformation of avian receptors (Stevens et al., 2006; Ha et al., 2001, 2003; Gamblin et al., 2004; Liu et al., 2009; Xu et al., 2010; Yang et al., 2010; Lin et al., 2012; Yang et al., 2012; Zhang et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to Stevens et al., 2006; Ha et al., 2001, 2003; Gamblin et al., 2004; Liu et al., 2009; Xu et al., 2010; Yang et al., 2010; Lin et al., 2012; Yang et al., 2012; Zhang et al., 2013

claim: Avian-adapted HAs typically carry Glu at position 190, Gln at position 226, and Gly at position 228 (H3 numbering).
source: Avian-adapted HAs typically carry Glu at position 190, Gln at position 226, and Gly and position 228 (H3 numbering)
evidence: Based on sequence analysis of avian viruses

claim: The Gln226->Leu, Gly228->Ser substitutions have been associated with a switch to human receptor preference in HAs of H2, H3, and H5 viruses.
source: and the Gln226->Leu, Gly228->Ser substitutions have been associated with a switch to human receptor preference in HAs of H2, H3 (Matrosovich et al., 2000), and H5 (Chutinimitkul et al., 2010) viruses.
evidence: Supported by citations to Matrosovich et al., 2000 and Chutinimitkul et al., 2010

claim: In H1 HA, Glu190→Asp and Gly225→Asp have been considered as hallmark amino acid changes to switch receptor specificity leading to greater human adaptation.
source: In H1 HA, Glu190→Asp and Gly225→Asp have been considered as hallmark amino acid changes to switch receptor specificity leading to greater human adaptation (Glaser et al., 2005; Tumpey et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to Glaser et al., 2005; Tumpey et al., 2007

claim: The cis and trans definition of glycan conformation does not fully describe HA binding to a range of structurally diverse glycans displayed on human respiratory cells and tissues.
source: The cis and trans definition of glycan conformation does not fully describe HA binding to a range of structurally diverse glycans displayed on human respiratory cells and tissues (Chandrasekaran et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to Chandrasekaran et al., 2008

claim: Studies have revisited the definition of glycan conformation, extending the conformational analysis beyond the terminal sialic acid linkage to describe overall topology and dynamics of the glycan receptor upon binding to the receptor-binding site of avian and human-adapted HAs.
source: This limitation motivated studies that revisited the definition of glycan conformation, extending the conformational analysis beyond the terminal sialic acid linkage to describe overall topology and dynamics of the glycan receptor upon binding to the receptor-binding site of avian and human-adapted HAs (Chandrasekaran et al., 2008; Xu et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to Chandrasekaran et al., 2008; Xu et al., 2009

claim: Experimental evidence on differential binding of avian and human viruses to sialic acid receptors in avian and human conformations was first obtained by hemagglutination assays with erythrocytes whose surfaces had been chemically modified.
source: Experimental evidence on differential binding of avian and human viruses to sialic acid receptors in avian and human conformations, respectively, was first obtained by hemagglutination assays with erythrocytes whose surfaces had been chemically modified to display glycans terminating with either homogeneous α2,3 or homogeneous α2,6-linked sialic acids (Paulson and Rogers, 1987).
evidence: Supported by citation to Paulson and Rogers, 1987

claim: Analysis of the repertoire of glycan structures in erythrocytes of various animal species informed the use of cells from different species as probes of HA receptor binding preference in hemagglutination assays.
source: Subsequent analysis of the repertoire of glycan structures in erythrocytes of various animal species informed the use of cells from different species as probes of HA receptor binding preference in hemagglutination assays (Ito et al., 1997).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ito et al., 1997

claim: Greater precision and reproducibility has been achieved with the use of purified sialylated glycans to create solid-phase binding assays with fluorogenic or enzymatic detection.
source: Greater precision and reproducibility has been achieved with the use of purified sialylated glycans to create solid-phase binding assays with fluorogenic or enzymatic detection (Gambaryan et al., 2006; Gambaryan and Matrosovich, 1992).
evidence: Supported by citations to Gambaryan et al., 2006; Gambaryan and Matrosovich, 1992

claim: Biosensor interferometry and thermophoresis have been used to measure glycan-binding avidities and affinities in a more precise manner.
source: In recent work, biosensor interferometry and thermophoresis have been used to measure glycan-binding avidities and affinities in a more precise manner and to relate the two (Xiong et al., 2013a).
evidence: Supported by citation to Xiong et al., 2013a

claim: The development of glycan microarrays represented a turning point in the analysis of influenza virus receptor binding specificity.
source: The development of glycan microarrays represented a turning point in the analysis of influenza virus receptor binding specificity, because it allowed simultaneous evaluation of virion or recombinant HA binding to a large repertoire of sialoglycans (Stevens et al., 2006; Blixt et al., 2004; Childs et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to Stevens et al., 2006; Blixt et al., 2004; Childs et al., 2009

claim: Glycans tested on current arrays may not match those present in the human respiratory tract.
source: A limitation to predictive power is that glycans tested on current arrays may not match those present in the human respiratory tract (Walther et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Walther et al., 2013

claim: Hallmark residues have substantial predictive power for receptor binding preference.
source: As noted above, hallmark residues have substantial predictive power. These distinct sets of hallmark residues in the H1, H2 and H3 subtype (Paulson and de Vries, 2013) correlate with human-adaptation in known sequences collected from birds or humans (Connor et al., 1994; Paulson and de Vries, 2013); they induce changes in receptor-binding specificity when introduced experimentally (Chen et al., 2012; Leigh et al., 1995); and experimental selection for receptor binding in vitro (Chen et al., 2012) or in ferrets (Imai et al., 2012) cause these changes to appear.
evidence: Supported by citations to Paulson and de Vries, 2013; Connor et al., 1994; Chen et al., 2012; Leigh et al., 1995; Imai et al., 2012

claim: Hallmark residue predictions of receptor-binding specificity are imperfect.
source: However, hallmark residue predictions of receptor-binding specificity are imperfect, as evidenced by a failure to switch in vitro receptor-binding preference from avian to human when changes observed in H5N1 strains after selection in ferret gain-of-function experiments were introduced to other H5N1 viruses (Tharakaraman et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Tharakaraman et al., 2013

claim: Several viruses circulating in humans during the early phase of previous pandemics were found to show either a preference for avian receptors or a mixed preference for both human and avian receptors.
source: Several viruses circulating in humans during the early phase of previous pandemics were found to show either a preference for avian receptors (Rogers and D'Souza, 1989; Connor et al., 1994) or a mixed preference for both human and avian receptors (Rogers and D'Souza, 1989; Glaser et al., 2005; Childs et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to Rogers and D'Souza, 1989; Connor et al., 1994; Glaser et al., 2005; Childs et al., 2009

claim: Some of the findings of dual or avian specificity may reflect artifacts introduced when human isolates were passaged in eggs before receptor specificity was assayed.
source: Some of the findings of dual or avian specificity may reflect artifacts introduced when human isolates were passaged in eggs before receptor specificity was assayed; alternatively, they may genuinely reflect a transitional stage in the evolution of HA genes in human populations after transmission from other species (Connor et al., 1994; Stevens et al., 2006; Glaser et al., 2005; Stevens et al., 2010)
evidence: Supported by citations to Connor et al., 1994; Stevens et al., 2006; Glaser et al., 2005; Stevens et al., 2010 and speculation

claim: An H5N1 virus isolated from a human zoonotic case in Vietnam displayed strong avian receptor preference.
source: Consistent with this latter possibility, an H5N1 virus isolated from a human zoonotic case in Vietnam displayed strong avian receptor preference (Yamada et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to Yamada et al., 2006

claim: The receptor preference of an H5N1 virus from a human case changed in the course of experiments to adapt it to respiratory droplet transmission in ferrets.
source: This preference changed in the course of experiments to adapt it to respiratory droplet transmission in ferrets (Imai et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Imai et al., 2012

claim: Detection of a human receptor preference in a spillover virus may be an indication of increased risk.
source: In summary, detection of a human receptor preference in a spillover virus may be an indication of increased risk, but exclusive human receptor preference is probably not necessary for an influenza A virus to initiate a pandemic.
evidence: Inferred from the evidence presented about receptor preference in pandemic viruses

claim: Exclusive human receptor preference is probably not necessary for an influenza A virus to initiate a pandemic.
source: In summary, detection of a human receptor preference in a spillover virus may be an indication of increased risk, but exclusive human receptor preference is probably not necessary for an influenza A virus to initiate a pandemic.
evidence: Inferred from examples of pandemic viruses with mixed receptor preference

claim: After entry into the cell, influenza viruses are internalized into endosomes, where the pH is progressively decreased.
source: After entry into the cell, influenza viruses are internalized into endosomes, where the pH is progressively decreased.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of cellular biology

claim: The HA must undergo a low-pH triggered conformational change to a state capable of fusing the viral and endosomal membranes.
source: The HA must undergo a low-pH triggered conformational change to a state capable of fusing the viral and endosomal membranes.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of influenza virus entry

claim: For human-adapted viruses, HA activation typically occurs between pH 5.0 to 5.5.
source: For human-adapted viruses, HA activation typically occurs between pH 5.0 to 5.5.
evidence: Based on measurements of human-adapted viruses

claim: HA variants that undergo the conformational transition at a higher pH are poorly adapted to infect human cells because the transition can happen prematurely, leading to extracellular inactivation in the mildly acidic mammalian respiratory tract.
source: HA variants that undergo this transition at a higher pH, as is typical for avian influenza isolates, are poorly adapted to infect human cells because the transition can happen prematurely, leading to extracellular inactivation in the mildly acidic mammalian respiratory tract (Di Lella et al., 2016; Zaraket et al., 2013a)
evidence: Supported by citations to Di Lella et al., 2016; Zaraket et al., 2013a

claim: Greater acid stability (lower pH of activation) is associated with greater human adaptation.
source: Greater acid stability (lower pH of activation) is associated with greater human adaptation.
evidence: Inferred from the relationship between pH of activation and human infection

claim: If the virion is exposed to sufficiently low pH outside of a host or host cell, the HA protein undergoes irreversible structural changes too early and is unable to mediate virus entry.
source: If the virion is exposed to sufficiently low pH outside of a host or host cell, the HA protein undergoes irreversible structural changes too early and is unable to mediate virus entry; such virions become inactivated.
evidence: Based on understanding of HA structure and function

claim: During endocytosis, an influenza virion is exposed to sequentially lower pH values in early endosomes (pH 6.0–6.5), late endosomes (pH 5.0–5.5), and lysosomes (pH 4.6–5.0).
source: During endocytosis, an influenza virion is exposed to sequentially lower pH values in early endosomes (pH 6.0–6.5), late endosomes (pH 5.0–5.5), and lysosomes (pH 4.6–5.0) (Mellman et al., 1986).
evidence: Supported by citation to Mellman et al., 1986

claim: If the HA is too stable, and fusion is not triggered in the acidic endosome of the host cell, further traffic into lysosomes results in virus inactivation by lysosomal proteases.
source: If the HA is too stable, and fusion is not triggered in the acidic endosome of the host cell, further traffic into lysosomes results in virus inactivation by lysosomal proteases (Skehel and Wiley, 2000).
evidence: Supported by citation to Skehel and Wiley, 2000

claim: Human-transmissible influenza isolates appear to have HA proteins that are more acid stable (have a lower activation pH) than avian influenza viruses.
source: Based on surveillance studies, human-transmissible influenza isolates appear to have HA proteins that are more acid stable (have a lower activation pH) than avian influenza viruses (Russell, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Russell, 2014

claim: The HA activation pH values for H1N1, H2N2, and H3N2 seasonal viruses during the 20th Century range from pH 5.0 to 5.4.
source: The HA activation pH values for H1N1, H2N2, and H3N2 seasonal viruses during the 20th Century range from pH 5.0 to 5.4 (Galloway et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Galloway et al., 2013

claim: In 2009, emerging pandemic H1N1 viruses had HA activation pH values of approximately 5.5.

source: One approach that has received considerable attention recently is to perform gain-of-transmissibility studies in highly pathogenic avian viruses; this has been controversial because of concerns about the unusual biosafety and biosecurity risks entailed in such studies (for contrasting perspectives on these risks, see the exchange in 2014–5 between Lipsitch and Inglesby, and Fouchier [Lipsitch and Inglesby, 2014, 2015; Fouchier, 2015]).
evidence: Supported by citations to Lipsitch and Inglesby, 2014, 2015; Fouchier, 2015

claim: Experiments starting from avian viruses that are not highly pathogenic in mammals can provide the same degree of causal rigor as gain-of-function in highly pathogenic avian viruses.
source: One alternative is to perform similar experiments starting from avian viruses that are not highly pathogenic in mammals, and/or are related to currently circulating human seasonal viruses, so that immunity would already be present in the population. Such experiments can provide the same degree of causal rigor as gain-of-function in highly pathogenic avian viruses with novel surface antigens and can elucidate general principles of mammalian adaptation, but they cannot confirm that the same changes would be observed in other strains that are not used in the experiment.
evidence: Reasoning about alternative experimental approaches

claim: A recent report shows the recreation of the steps of mammalian adaptation using viruses whose HA and NA are already circulating in humans.
source: A recent report shows a related way forward: the recreation of the steps of mammalian adaptation using viruses whose HA and NA are already circulating in humans (Lakdawala et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lakdawala et al., 2015

claim: A 2011 report demonstrated the importance of HA activation pH in mouse adaptation by selection experiments on a live attenuated H5N1 vaccine strain lacking the NS1 gene.
source: A 2011 report employed a similar strategy, demonstrating the importance of HA activation pH in mouse adaptation by selection experiments on a live attenuated H5N1 vaccine strain lacking the NS1 gene (Krenn et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Krenn et al., 2011

claim: A 2009 H1N1 pandemic virus was modified to express a mutation that increased pH of HA activation, then selected in ferrets for droplet transmission, and it was found that a second site mutation partially restored the lower pH of activation.
source: More recently, a 2009 H1N1 pandemic virus was modified to express a mutation that increased pH of HA activation, then selected in ferrets for droplet transmission, and it was found that a second site mutation partially restored the lower pH of activation of the selected virus (Russier et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Russier et al., 2016

claim: One limitation of de-adaptation strategies is that the acquisition of transmissibility is perhaps most likely to evolve by reversion of the de-adaptation changes.
source: One limitation of de-adaptation strategies is that the acquisition of transmissibility is perhaps most likely to evolve by reversion of the de-adaptation changes.
evidence: Logical reasoning about experimental design limitations

claim: Epistatic effects of other loci in the genetic background of viruses used in gain-of-function and loss-of-function studies set limits to the generalizability of such experiments.
source: As with all gain-of-function and loss-of-function studies, epistatic effects of other loci in the genetic background of the viruses used in such studies set limits to the generalizability of such experiments.
evidence: Reasoning about limitations of experimental approaches

claim: Surveillance is a key rate-limiting step for pandemic risk assessment to direct countermeasure development.
source: Even if strain-based assessment methods were much better, surveillance would be a key rate-limiting step for pandemic risk assessment to direct countermeasure development.
evidence: Logical reasoning about the importance of surveillance

claim: We have yet to identify a pandemic strain in nonhuman hosts or in human spillover cases before the pandemic starts.
source: The fact that we have yet to identify a pandemic strain in nonhuman hosts or in human spillover cases before the pandemic starts indicates there is much work to be done.
evidence: Based on historical observation

claim: Surveillance has expanded since the 2009 pandemic.
source: Although surveillance has expanded since the 2009 pandemic, it has not been designed to optimize the chances of detecting a pandemic strain before it becomes pandemic; indeed, how to do so is not clear at present.
evidence: Based on knowledge of surveillance efforts

claim: Careful attention to passage histories of surveillance isolates is needed to avoid altering their genotype and phenotype post-isolation.
source: The uncertainties noted above about the phenotypic characteristics of viruses isolated from previous pandemics (which may have been present in the primary isolate or may have arisen during egg passage in the laboratory) underline the need for careful attention to passage histories of surveillance isolates to avoid altering their genotype and phenotype post-isolation (Bush et al., 2000).
evidence: Supported by citation to Bush et al., 2000 and logical reasoning

claim: It may be improbable that we can reliably identify the 'needle in the haystack' that is the next pandemic influenza strain.
source: Even with all of the foregoing suggestions in place, it may be improbable that we can reliably identify the 'needle in the haystack' that is the next pandemic influenza strain.
evidence: Speculation about the limits of prediction

claim: The goal is not risk assessment for its own sake, but preparedness and early response to pandemic threats.
source: Ultimately, the goal is not risk assessment for its own sake, but preparedness and early response to pandemic threats.
evidence: Statement of public health objectives

claim: Making and improving predictions should be accompanied by a systematic effort to design responses that will not fail even if the predictions are wrong.
source: In other areas where security is at stake, it has been argued that making and improving predictions should be accompanied by a systematic effort to design responses that will not fail even if the predictions are wrong (Danzig, 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Danzig, 2011

claim: The value of some countermeasures is strongly reliant on our ability to identify truly high-risk prepandemic threats.
source: In the influenza context, the value of some countermeasures is strongly reliant on our ability to identify truly high-risk prepandemic threats: notably, preparation of seed vaccine stocks for candidate pandemic strains, stockpiling of subtype-specific vaccines, and culling of poultry infected with such strains.
evidence: Reasoning about the relationship between prediction and countermeasures

claim: Other types of countermeasures should provide benefits whether or not we have advance notice of the strain causing the next pandemic.
source: Other types of countermeasures, ranging from strengthening local public health departments to stockpiling antivirals or ventilators to developing faster processes for vaccine manufacture to universal vaccines that should be effective against any influenza A strain, should provide benefits whether or not we have advance notice of the strain causing the next pandemic.
evidence: Reasoning about robust countermeasures

claim: A comprehensive assessment of priorities to prevent or mitigate the next influenza pandemic should consider the balance between improving risk assessment capacity and developing responses robust to the possibility of being caught by surprise.
source: A comprehensive assessment of priorities to prevent or mitigate the next influenza pandemic should consider the balance between improving our risk assessment capacity and developing responses robust to the possibility that we will once again be caught by surprise.
evidence: Recommendation based on the analysis in the review
